parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A student opens a bank account.
script: Good morning. How can I help you?
Hi. I'm a new student here, and I'd like to open a bank account.
Of course. Can I have your full name?
Lena Kowalski. K, O, W, A, L, S, K, I.
Then I'd recommend our student account. There's no monthly fee, and you can have an overdraft of up to five hundred pounds without paying interest.
That sounds good. What documents do you need?
Your passport, and a letter from the university confirming that you're a student.
Perfect. Your debit card will arrive by post in about five working days.
You can download our app straight away, but your password will be sent separately by post, for security reasons.
OK. Is this branch open at weekends?
Yes, on Saturdays from nine thirty until one.
Great. Could I also speak to someone about money transfers from Poland?
Certainly. Our adviser is available on Friday afternoon. Shall I book you an appointment?

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: An information officer talks about ferry services to a group of islands.
script: Good morning, and thank you for coming. I'm Morag from Island Ferries, and I'd like to tell you about our services this summer and the islands you can visit.

First, the timetable has changed. In the past, ferries left at fixed times regardless of other transport. From this year, departures have been changed to match the arrival of trains from the city, so you won't have long waits at the harbour.
Tickets are no longer sold on board. You'll need to buy them online in advance. The harbour office is now only for information.
You can take a bicycle on any ferry, but there's a small charge of two pounds each way.
If the weather is too bad for sailing, we'll send everyone with a booking a text message as early as possible.
Now, the islands. On Inchmore, the old lighthouse has been restored, and you can climb to the top and visit the keeper's cottage.
Seal Island is the best place for watching wildlife. As well as seals, you'll see puffins and many other seabirds.
Long Isle has a beautiful sandy beach that's safe for swimming, with lifeguards in July and August.
Craig Rock is closed to visitors in spring, from March to May, while birds are nesting.
On Holm, there's a small campsite, which is very popular, so do book early.
And finally, Eilean Mor has the only café on the islands, run by the local community, and it's famous for its homemade cakes.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: A student, Jack, discusses his essay on fast fashion with his tutor, Dr Moreno.
script: Hello Jack. I've read your draft essay on fast fashion. There's a lot to like here.
Thanks. I wasn't sure about the structure.
The structure is fine, actually. What really impressed me was your use of statistics. You support almost every point with data.
But the main weakness is that it's too descriptive. You explain what fast fashion is very well, but you don't really argue a position. I want to know what you think should be done.
I see. I'll add a section on that.
Also, your figure on water use comes from a fashion magazine. It may be accurate, but you need a more reliable source, such as a report from the United Nations.
OK. I'll find the original report.
And you're five hundred words over the limit, so you'll need to cut some of the background.
Is there any chance of an extension?
I'm afraid not. It's still due on Friday.
Right. Let me check the key figures I'm going to keep. The fashion industry produces up to ten percent of global carbon emissions.
That's the commonly quoted upper estimate, yes. Make sure you say it's an estimate.
Making one cotton T-shirt uses about two thousand seven hundred litres of water.
The average garment is worn only seven times before it's thrown away. And less than one percent of clothing is recycled into new clothes.
Good. And you mention the Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh?
Yes, in 2013, when more than eleven hundred workers died.

options: The source is not reliable enough.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on designing buildings to survive earthquakes.
script: Good morning. Today we're going to look at how engineers design buildings to survive earthquakes.

It's often said that earthquakes don't kill people; buildings do. Most deaths in earthquakes are caused by collapsing buildings rather than by the shaking of the ground itself. So the design of buildings is crucial.

One of the most effective techniques is base isolation. The building sits on bearings made of layers of rubber and steel. When the ground shakes, these bearings allow the ground to move sideways beneath the building, while the building itself moves much less.
Another technique uses dampers, which work rather like the shock absorbers in a car. They absorb some of the energy of the movement and reduce swaying.

A famous example is Taipei 101, in Taiwan, which was once the tallest building in the world. Near the top hangs a huge steel ball, weighing six hundred and sixty tonnes. When the building sways, the ball moves in the opposite direction, reducing the movement.
Japan has some of the strictest building codes in the world. They were strengthened after the Kobe earthquake in 1995, which killed more than six thousand people and destroyed many older buildings.

But these advanced technologies are expensive. In developing countries, engineers have found cheaper methods. For example, walls can be reinforced by wrapping them in steel mesh and covering it with plaster.

Traditional building methods can also offer lessons. In Kashmir, houses built with flexible wooden frames filled with small pieces of stone survived earthquakes far better than modern concrete buildings.
The biggest challenge, however, is not new construction, but strengthening existing buildings, many of which were built before modern codes existed.

passages.title: The Sundarbans
paragraphs: Where the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers meet the Bay of Bengal lies the largest mangrove forest in the world, the Sundarbans. Covering around 10,000 square kilometres, it is shared between Bangladesh, which contains about sixty percent of the forest, and India. The name is generally thought to come from the sundari, a mangrove tree that is common in the region. The Bangladeshi part of the forest was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.

The Sundarbans is a constantly changing landscape of islands, mudflats and tidal channels, flooded twice a day by the sea. Mangrove trees are specially adapted to these conditions. Many have roots that grow upwards out of the mud, allowing them to take in oxygen, and they can tolerate salt water that would kill most plants.

The forest is best known for the Royal Bengal tiger. Unlike most tigers, those in the Sundarbans are strong swimmers, crossing wide rivers between islands, and they survive partly on fish and crabs. A survey in 2018 counted 114 tigers in the Bangladeshi part of the forest, a slight increase on the previous survey.

For the people who live around the forest, tigers are a real danger. Woodcutters, fishermen and honey collectors, known locally as mawals, enter the forest to earn a living, and each year some are attacked. Honey collectors traditionally work in groups and sometimes wear masks on the backs of their heads, in the belief that tigers prefer to attack from behind.

The Sundarbans also protects millions of people. When Cyclone Sidr struck Bangladesh in 2007, the forest acted as a natural barrier, reducing the force of the storm surge and the wind. The forest itself was badly damaged, but scientists believe the loss of life inland would have been far greater without it.

Today the forest faces several threats. Upstream dams and the diversion of river water have reduced the flow of fresh water, so the water in parts of the forest has become saltier. Rising salinity is affecting the growth of sundari trees, which prefer less salty conditions. Rising sea levels, caused by climate change, threaten to flood low-lying areas permanently. There has also been controversy over the construction of a large coal power plant near the forest, which environmental groups argue could pollute the air and water.

passages.title: Machines That Play Chess
paragraphs: Chess has a long history. Its earliest known ancestor is chaturanga, a game played in India around the sixth century AD, whose pieces represented the divisions of an army. The game spread to Persia and then, through the Islamic world, to Europe, where by the fifteenth century it had developed into a form very close to modern chess.

For centuries, chess was seen as a supreme test of human intelligence, and the idea of a machine that could play it fascinated people. In 1770, the Hungarian inventor Wolfgang von Kempelen presented the Mechanical Turk, a life-sized figure seated at a cabinet, which appeared to play chess by itself. It toured Europe and America for decades, defeating many opponents. In reality, it was a hoax: a skilled human player was hidden inside the cabinet.

The first real chess program was written before a computer existed that could run it. In 1950 the mathematician Alan Turing wrote a set of rules for playing chess and, lacking a suitable machine, carried out the calculations himself with pencil and paper. Each move took him around half an hour, and the program lost its only recorded game.

The decisive moment came in 1997, when IBM's computer Deep Blue defeated the world champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match. Deep Blue did not think like a human. Its strength came from enormous calculating power: it could evaluate around 200 million positions per second, searching through possible sequences of moves far more deeply than any person could.

Twenty years later, a very different program showed another way. In 2017, the company DeepMind revealed AlphaZero, which was given only the rules of chess and then learned by playing millions of games against itself. Within hours of starting, it was strong enough to defeat the best existing chess programs. Professional players were struck by its creative, attacking style, which seemed more human than the cautious play of earlier machines.

Many people predicted that once computers became stronger than humans, interest in chess would decline. The opposite has happened. Chess is more popular than ever, with millions of games played online every day, and players at every level use computers to study and improve. Some enthusiasts have even experimented with 'centaur' chess, in which teams made up of a human and a computer compete against each other, combining human judgement with machine calculation.

passages.title: Should We Abolish Cash?
paragraphs: In many countries, notes and coins are disappearing from everyday life. Sweden has gone further than almost anywhere else: cash is now used in fewer than one in ten purchases in shops, many cafés and even some banks no longer accept it, and most Swedes pay with cards or a mobile payment app. Several other countries, from the United Kingdom to China, are moving in the same direction. Some economists argue that cash should be abolished altogether.

Supporters of a cashless society point to clear benefits. Digital payments are fast and convenient, and they reduce the costs of printing, transporting and protecting cash. Crime may also fall: in Sweden, the number of bank robberies has declined dramatically as banks hold less cash. Because digital transactions leave a record, they also make it harder to hide income from tax authorities, reducing tax evasion and money laundering.

Some governments have tried to speed up the change. In 2016, India suddenly withdrew its two highest-value banknotes, which made up most of the cash in circulation, in an attempt to fight corruption and tax evasion. The decision caused severe disruption, with long queues at banks and serious problems for small businesses, but it also led to rapid growth in digital payments, which have since become part of daily life for hundreds of millions of people.

Yet a completely cashless society carries real risks. The first is exclusion. Many elderly people find digital payments confusing, and some people in rural areas have poor internet access or no bank account. For them, the disappearance of cash can make it difficult to buy basic goods. Sweden has recognised this problem: since 2021, its largest banks have been required by law to provide cash services across the country.

A second concern is resilience. If payments depend entirely on electronic systems, a power cut, technical failure or cyberattack could leave people unable to buy food or medicine. Swedish authorities now advise households to keep some cash at home in case of emergencies. A third concern is privacy. Every digital payment creates a record of what was bought, where and when, and this information can be collected by companies or governments.

In my view, the decline of cash is natural and largely positive, but abolishing it would be a mistake. Cash remains the only form of payment that works without electricity, does not require a bank account and leaves no data trail. Governments should not force people to use it, but they should ensure that it remains widely accepted and easily available for those who need or prefer it.

task1.text: The table below shows the average number of hours per week that men and women in one country spent on four household tasks in 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

chart.title: Hours per week spent on household tasks

model: The table compares the average weekly time that men and women in one country spent on cooking, cleaning, childcare and shopping in 2000 and 2020.
Overall, women spent more time than men on every task in both years. However, the gap narrowed considerably over the period, as men did more housework and women did slightly less.

In 2000, women spent the most time on childcare, at 10 hours a week, followed by cooking at 9 hours and cleaning at 7 hours. Men's contributions were much smaller: 3 hours each on cooking and childcare, 2 hours on cleaning and just 1.5 hours on shopping.

By 2020, the time men spent on each task had increased, doubling for cleaning and childcare to 4 and 6 hours respectively, and rising to 5 hours for cooking. In contrast, women's figures fell slightly across all four tasks, for example from 9 to 7 hours for cooking. As a result, the difference between men and women in cooking time fell from 6 hours to only 2 hours.

task2.text: The clothing industry causes serious damage to the environment. Some people think consumers should be responsible for reducing this damage, while others believe it is the responsibility of companies and governments. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
model: The fashion industry is a major source of pollution, waste and carbon emissions, and it is widely agreed that something must change. There is less agreement about who should lead that change. In my view, consumers have a role to play, but the main responsibility lies with companies and governments.

Those who emphasise consumer responsibility argue that the industry simply responds to demand. If people bought fewer, better-quality clothes, repaired them and bought second-hand, fast fashion brands would have to change their business models. Individuals can also make a difference by choosing companies that use sustainable materials and treat workers fairly. From this perspective, every purchase is a kind of vote.

However, there are limits to what consumers can do. Many people, especially those on low incomes, cannot afford more expensive sustainable clothing. Moreover, shoppers rarely have reliable information about how and where their clothes were made, and companies spend enormous sums on marketing designed to encourage frequent buying. It seems unfair to expect individuals to solve a problem that is built into the way the industry operates.

Companies and governments have far greater power. Manufacturers control the materials they use, the conditions in their factories and the amount they produce. Governments can set rules, for example by requiring companies to take responsibility for recycling their products, banning the destruction of unsold clothing, or taxing the most polluting materials. Such measures affect the whole industry at once.

In conclusion, although consumers should make responsible choices where they can, I believe meaningful change depends on companies changing how they produce clothes and on governments setting clear rules to make sustainable practices the norm.

speaking.cue:
Describe a skill you would like to learn in the future.
You should say:
- what the skill is
- how you would learn it
- how long you think it would take
and explain why you want to learn it.
speaking.cueModel: One skill I'd really like to learn is scuba diving. I've always loved the ocean, and when I've snorkelled in clear water, I've always wished I could go deeper and stay there longer. I think I'd learn it properly, through a recognised diving course, rather than just trying it on holiday. The usual way is to take an open water course, which starts with theory lessons and practice in a swimming pool, and then finishes with several dives in the sea with an instructor. From what I've read, the basic course only takes three or four days, but becoming genuinely confident would take much longer, probably a few years of regular diving. There are a few reasons I want to learn it. The first is simply curiosity. I've seen documentaries about coral reefs and I'd love to see that world with my own eyes. I'm also interested in marine conservation, and divers can take part in projects that monitor reefs and clean up plastic. And finally, I like the idea of doing something that's a bit challenging. Breathing underwater must feel very strange at first, and I'd like to prove to myself that I can stay calm and do it.
